course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Globalization
unit.description: Study how technology, disease, and environmental change reshaped the world, how the global economy and culture developed, and how people and institutions responded to globalization.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Bill Clinton, president of the United States, State of the Union address to Congress, January 27, 2000
stimulusBlocks.citation: William J. Clinton, Address Before a Joint Session of the Congress on the State of the Union, January 27, 2000. Text checked against the C-SPAN transcript in the NLTK corpus (state_union/2000-Clinton.txt).
stimulusBlocks.note: Two months earlier, tens of thousands of protesters had disrupted a World Trade Organization meeting in Seattle.
stimulusBlocks.text:
To realize the full possibilities of this economy, we must reach beyond our own borders, to shape the revolution that is tearing down barriers and building new networks among nations and individuals and economies and cultures: globalization. It's the central reality of our time.

Of course, change this profound is both liberating and threatening to people. But there's no turning back. . . .

The first thing we have got to do is to forge a new consensus on trade. Now, those of us who believe passionately in the power of open trade, we have to ensure that it lifts both our living standards and our values, never tolerating abusive child labor or a race to the bottom in the environment and worker protection. But others must recognize that open markets and rule-based trade are the best engines we know of for raising living standards, reducing global poverty and environmental destruction, and assuring the free flow of ideas.

questions.prompt: In the passage, Clinton argues that open trade
choices: should be abandoned in favor of tariffs
can raise living standards and reduce poverty
has no effect on the environment at all
threatens no one's jobs or way of life
questions.explanation: He calls open markets the best engines for raising living standards.
choiceExplanations: He says there is no turning back.
He calls open markets the best engines for raising living standards.
He mentions environmental protection.
He says change is threatening to people.
questions.distinguisher: Clinton admits globalization is “threatening” to some people.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 9.7 key concept: movements emerged that resisted economic globalization and its effects
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing resistance to globalization, 1994–2001
stimulusBlocks.text:
On January 1, 1994, the day the North American Free Trade Agreement took effect, the Zapatista Army of National Liberation rose up in Chiapas, Mexico. The rebels, mostly Indigenous farmers, argued that free trade would destroy small farmers who could not compete with cheap imported corn.

In 1999, tens of thousands of labor union members, environmentalists, and students protested a World Trade Organization meeting in Seattle. In 2001, activists founded the World Social Forum in Brazil under the slogan “Another world is possible.”

questions.prompt: The passage would best support which argument about resistance to globalization?
choices: It united diverse groups
It was limited to Mexico
It supported the WTO
It ended in 1994
questions.explanation: Farmers, unions, environmentalists, and students joined.
choiceExplanations: Farmers, unions, environmentalists, and students joined.
It spread to Seattle and Brazil.
Protesters opposed the WTO.
It continued into 2001.
questions.distinguisher: It began in Mexico but spread to the United States and Brazil.

questions.prompt: Which concern about NAFTA did the Zapatistas express?
choices: That the agreement would raise taxes on factories
That cheap imported corn would harm small farmers
That it would end Mexico's oil exports to the United States
That it would ban the sale of Mexican corn abroad
questions.explanation: The Zapatistas argued that competition from imported corn would hurt small farmers.
choiceExplanations: The passage does not mention taxes on factories.
The Zapatistas argued that competition from imported corn would hurt small farmers.
The passage names cheap imported corn, not oil, as the Zapatistas' concern.
The concern was about imports, not a ban on exports.
questions.distinguisher: NAFTA did affect Mexican trade, but the Zapatistas' stated concern was imported crops.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 9.7 key concept: groups resisted globalization, defending local economies and cultures
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Zapatista uprising, 1994
stimulusBlocks.text:
On January 1, 1994, the day the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) took effect, a rebel group calling itself the Zapatista Army of National Liberation seized several towns in the southern Mexican state of Chiapas. Its members were mostly Indigenous Maya farmers. They demanded land, better schools and health care, and political rights, and they argued that NAFTA would harm small farmers by exposing them to competition from cheap imported corn.

After about twelve days of fighting, the Mexican government declared a cease-fire and began talks. The Zapatistas used the internet and the international press to spread their message, and the movement became a symbol for critics of globalization around the world.

questions.prompt: The Zapatistas' use of the internet and international press shows that
choices: globalization had not yet reached Mexico by 1994
the Mexican government controlled all news and information
only governments had the means to use global communications
global technology could be used by critics of globalization
questions.explanation: The movement spread its message widely using global communications.
choiceExplanations: NAFTA took effect in 1994, which shows Mexico was affected.
The Zapatistas reached international audiences.
A rebel group used the internet.
The movement spread its message widely using global communications.
questions.distinguisher: Governments had more resources, but the passage shows a small movement also reaching world audiences.
